September 2009 ## **Will the greenfields of Peru replace the brownfields of Chile? - Profiling the next generation of copper mine projects** The rebound in the copper price has been encouraging companies to take a second look at their project portfolios. Some major companies have announced new discoveries, while some juniors are seeking finance. Codelco’s Salvador Division (Chile) presented an Environmental Assessment for the San Antonio project, which would prolong operations at Salvador for a further 20 years. The existing Salvador mine was due to close by 2011. Anglo American announced significant discoveries at Los Sulfatos and San Enrique Monolito adjacent to Los Bronces mines (Chile). Antofagasta’s Esperanza project is starting-up Q4 2010 and is the flagship of the next generation of greenfield projects to come on stream. CRU has carried out a detailed research of 98 projects worldwide through 131 project profiles (Copper Mines Project Profiles – 2009 edition) and some important findings for South America are: - There are 48 copper mine projects (including new mines and expansions) in South America which CRU has identified in 58 profiles. This puts the region at the top of the ranking of new developments. Within South America and the world, Chile has the largest number of projects. - There are 20 firm/committed projects in South America. Esperanza is the region’s flagship project due to start-up next year. It has competitive advantages over other new developments, including low economic cost, low unit capex and prompt start-up. - Production capacity of the 85 projects is higher than existing operations. Amongst the projects, brownfield expansions will account for a larger proportion of new capacity than greenfield projects (especially in Chile). © 2009 CRU International Limited **confidential** **September 2009** **www.crumonitor.com** ## **How many projects are out there?** There are 39 greenfield and 19 brownfield (expansions or extensions) projects in the portfolio of copper developments in South America that CRU includes into its new study. South America leads the world’s copper production potential over the next years, followed by North America. Chile has the greatest production potential in South America (1,995kt of contained copper – considering 100% probability for firm projects, 50% for probable Copper projects in South America projects and 25% for possible projects) and also the number of new mines and expansions/extensions, from 2009 onward largest number of new developments in South America. Notwithstanding, reserves at many of the current operations in Chile are being depleted so these projects, **Chile** in part, will offset this depletion. For example, the San Antonio project at Salvador Division will start-up once **Peru** current operations end in 2011. Copper projects in South America

Many of these projects are held by major companies as they require large capital investments of over US$1B on average. However, rising capital cost for building open pit mines to produce copper in concentrate, which is the project type that dominates in South America, have the highest capex compared to the other types of mine and this is putting pressure on capital competitiveness. The largest firm project, Esperanza (Chile) – owned by Antofagasta Minerals (70%) and Marubeni Corporation (30%) – is under construction and requires a capital investment of US$2.34B. This capex may seem high, but in fact is highly competitive as it includes concentrate and water pipelines from the coast to the mine site, plus two Data: CRU Analysis © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 6 **September 2009** www.crumonitor.com desalination plants. The rock mined will have an average stripping ratio of 3.08:1 and the concentrator will process 35.5Mt of ore. At full capacity production will be around 191,000t/y of copper in concentrate. Esperanza’s target diagram reflects a low grade, open pit project and a deposit relatively small for Chile, but typical of the newer projects in the country. The main competitive advantage of this project is that its start-up date (Q4 2010) takes gains of expected high price levels over

the next few years. ## **The challenges of developing a large copper mine** Brownfield projects show, on average, higher production levels than new (greenfield) mines. There is a world trend to exploit new deposits in a number of stages rather than construct a mega project; which allows companies to break down the capex into more manageable stages. Other reasons of this are because most sulphides (processed into copper concentrates) lie below oxide bodies (usually leached to produce copper cathodes) or because deposits contain mineralisation that requires new technologies to be economically exploitable. Many of these new mines are larger deposits with lower grades compared to projects developed during past decades. These projects will require more investment capital and will present technological challenges. In Chile, the overall average production level of its projects is 143,000t/y of copper. Expansions will account for a larger proportion of the tonnage, as they equal almost 50% of the 2008 Chilean production level. Most expansions are of existing operations, which will duplicate or replace current production levels. This seems a sensible reason to explain why Chile is showing the least delays. In Peru, most projects are new mines with an average production capacity of 150,000t/y of copper. Only five mines (Antamina, Cerro Verde, Toquepala, Cuajone and Tintaya) produce currently above 110,000t/y. Copper production average levels

# Copper production - In Chile, copper production decreased 1% y-o-y in June. This is the twelfth consecutive month of decline. The reasons are similar to those in May, April and March. Escondida alone produced 35,600t less because of lower ore grades and technical failures at its Laguna Seca SAG mill. This mill re-started on August 2nd , so Escondida’s production should increase from August. Codelco produced 27,800t more than in June 2008 mainly because of the Codelco Norte and the ramp-up at Gaby. All other operations in Chile remained at the same range. In July, according to the National Statistics Institute, copper production in Chile was 427,018t (-1.3% y-o-y). - In Peru, copper production increased 8% y-o-y in July. Cerro Verde’ copper in concentrates production declined by 29% to 15kt, and explains 6% (of the 8%) of the decline in the Peruvian copper production. In addition, as in previous months, the ramp-up at Cerro Corona (2.9kt more than in July 2008) partly offset the decline at Antamina (-5.0kt due to higher zinc and lower copper grades). © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 6 **September 2009** **www.crumonitor.com**
